prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Offshore, the Apocalypse stays contained to one island and its church. Venice's ruler's out wedding himself to the ocean while I'm ankle deep in the Adriatic, eyes raised to a book unencumbered by words: A Bible that reads from East to West. Guidebooks want only to see it as ceiling—the Basilica San Marco, where Christ's hands open on wounds embedded with rubies, and priests hold back the sea with brooms. I'm taking on incense, bowing at altars dragged out of Constantinople, sloshing across marble sacked from Jerusalem. Offshore, the sea's a bride bought with a fist full of diamonds the Doge throws into the deep— a sign of his true and perpetual dominion. Then why does walking into this church mean stepping into the ocean? The sea is a dog— Priests throw in bones just to placate it. The year's nearly 2000, but the millennium already hit once on the island Torcello, a kind of plague the Venetians contained. 999 years, and the dead still crawl from dirt towards their radiant bodies, they still gather up missing limbs: arms, legs, hands sharks and beasts keep regurgitating. We do what we know— But Christ never wanted to manage resurrections in Venice. Underdressed in the flesh from dead civilizations, he moves among us in Byzantine skin. I'm getting close to this God worshiped only by tourists. He picks at the wounds on his crucified body, the injury scabbed over with jewels.

### Option 1: Sophisticated Literary Prose (Recommended)

Beyond the coastline, apocalyptic chaos remains confined to a single island and its sanctuary. While Venice’s chief magistrate performs his symbolic matrimony with the sea, I stand in shallow Adriatic waters, looking up at a wordless visual text: a mosaic scripture designed to be read right-to-left. 

Tourist handbooks reduce St. Mark’s Cathedral to mere roof art, where Christ displays stigmata inlaid with rubies, and clergy attempt to push back floodwaters with simple brooms. Surrounded by sacred smoke, I bow before altars plundered from Constantinople and wade over marble slabs looted from Jerusalem. 

Out in the deep, the ocean acts as a bride bribed by handfuls of gems the ruler tosses into the waves to claim eternal authority. Yet entering this house of worship is indistinguishable from plunging into open water. The ocean resembles a hound, pacified only when ministers throw it scraps. 

As Y2K approaches, one recalls that an apocalyptic turn already struck Torcello centuries ago—a localized blight the Venetians managed to isolate. Almost a thousand years later, the departed still drag themselves from the earth toward glorified forms, reassembling missing limbs regurgitated by sharks and scavengers. 

We fall back on familiar routines, though Jesus never aimed to direct bodily resurrections in Venice. Clad in the physical remnants of fallen empires, he moves among the living wrapped in Byzantine style. I draw near to this divinity whom only sightseers now revere, watching him scratch at his crucifixion scars, which have healed over with precious stones.
outputs.L3:
For centuries, Venice defined its sovereign identity through a grand theatrical gesture: the Doge, aboard his golden barge, would cast a consecrated ring into the Adriatic, symbolically marrying the sea to assert absolute dominion over the waves. Yet this imperial arrogance has always been answered by a quiet, persistent rebellion. Despite the rituals of empire, the ocean refuses to be mastered. It regularly breaks its bounds, invading the marble heart of the city and drowning the floor of Basilica San Marco in brackish brine, a humid reminder that the bride will eventually consume her groom.

This threatened sanctuary is itself a monument built on the ashes of older worlds. Basilica San Marco is less a coherent architectural creation than a grand, holy reliquary of stolen majesty, physically constructed from the detritus of fallen empires. Its walls, altars, and columns are fashioned from *spolia*—marbles, porphyry, and sacred relics violently looted from the sacks of Constantinople and the holy sites of Jerusalem. Venice stitched together its own divine authority using the fragmented bones of the civilizations it crushed or outlived.

The darker, apocalyptic undercurrents of this Venetian reality are laid bare on the desolate nearby island of Torcello, the ancient, marshy predecessor to Venice itself. Inside its silent cathedral, a terrifying legacy lingers in the Byzantine mosaics of the Last Judgment. There, the resurrected dead symbolically rise from the earth and the sea, crawling back to life while wild beasts and sea monsters disgorgeth missing hands, legs, and heads so that the damned and the saved alike might reclaim their whole forms. It is a grotesque vision of salvation, where the act of reassembly is painful, visceral, and disturbing.

At the center of this grim theological landscape stands a distinctly Venetian-Byzantine vision of Christ. He is not rendered as a gentle shepherd, but as a stern, remote emperor rendered in shimmering gold *tesserae*. His holy wounds do not bleed; instead, they are depicted as rigid, jewel-encrusted badges of suffering. In this sunken world, Christ appears as a weary administrator of the supernatural, reluctantly overseeing the mechanical, messy burden of human resurrections amidst a city built on mud and stolen grace.

Ultimately, the terror, divine hubris, and bloody history that forged Venice have been drained of their apocalyptic weight. The sacred monuments that once struck dread into the hearts of medieval citizens and celebrated crushed empires have been hollowed out by time. Today, the horrific resurrections of Torcello and the jewel-wounded God of San Marco have transformed into mere backdrops. The profound paradoxes of a sinking holy empire are now consumed as a passive, fleeting spectacle, casually observed by crowds of tourists wading through the rising floodwaters with camera lenses raised.
outputs.L4:
The cold, brackish water of the Adriatic had crept past the marble threshold of the Basilica San Marco, transforming the ancient floor into a murky, shimmering mirror. I waded slowly through the dark nave, my rubber boots disturbing the quiet surface and sending small ripples against the bases of columns that had stood for nearly a thousand years. Above me, the golden Byzantine mosaics caught the dim, amber glow of emergency floodlights, reflecting off the rising tide below. To walk through San Marco during an *acqua alta* is to witness a sacred space being slowly reclaimed by the very element that once birthed its wealth, a stark confrontation with Venice’s impending existential collapse.

For centuries, Venice defied the odds of geography, building an empire of glass, stone, and gold upon the treacherous mudflats of a lagoon. But as I moved deeper into the flooded sanctuary, the water swirling at my knees offered a haunting reminder of how that empire was constructed. San Marco is less a house of pure devotion than a vaulted treasure chest of imperial plunder. The red porphyry pillars, the intricate floor mosaics, the famous bronze horses on the facade—and even the stolen bones of Saint Mark himself—were stripped from the falling ruins of Constantinople and the Levant during the Fourth Crusade. Venice built its grandeur on the spoils of war, hoarding jewels and relics as if they were talismans capable of ransoming the city from fate.

Yet, alongside this immense material arrogance ran a deep, neurotic strain of apocalyptic dread. As the sea now laps against the alabaster tombs, one can sense the ghost of that ancient anxiety. The medieval Venetians were obsessively aware of their fragile perch between earth and water, living in constant fear of divine wrath, plague, and catastrophic inundation. To ward off the inevitable, they devised elaborate civic and religious rituals: litanies read in the dark, solemn processions, and the grand annual ceremony of the *Sensa*, in which the Doge cast a gold ring into the sea to declare Venice’s eternal marriage to the Adriatic.

Looking at the jewel-encrusted icons submerged in the rising gloom—the famous *Pala d'Oro* glittering uselessly behind protective barricades—the tragic paradox of the city becomes painfully clear. These placating rituals and opulent icons were never truly about divine communion; they were instruments of psychological defense, a gilded theater designed to project an illusion of total control over forces that defy human mastery. 

Today, that theater has been commodified. Tourists in plastic ponchos snap photos of the flooded crypts, while ticket counters sell admission to view the gilded relics of a drowning museum. We have replaced holy terror with commercialized spectacle, yet the underlying hubris remains unchanged. We build high-tech floodgates and perform bureaucratic rites, clinging to the belief that human ingenuity and accumulated capital can permanently freeze a floating city in time.

As I reached the altar, the tide reached its peak, sloshing gently against the marble steps. The silence of the cathedral was broken only by the rhythmic hum of submerged sump pumps—a desperate, mechanical heartbeat fighting an impossible war. In the dark, rising water of San Marco, the illusion finally dissolves. Neither imperial loot, nor sacred gold, nor the arrogance of modern engineering can placate the sea. The Adriatic does not care for art history or empire; it merely claims what has always been its own, exposing the ultimate futility of mankind’s attempt to dominate nature and master time.
outputs.L5:
From the deck of Rig Zero, forty miles out in the Adriatic, the world looked like an endless expanse of gray steel and dark, iron-tasted water. 

When the Great Rising came, it was not the fire-and-brimstone apocalypse of ancient texts, but a slow, suffocating drowning. The polar ice dissolved, the rivers swelled, and the oceans reclaimed the coasts with a patient, unstoppable appetite. Humanity’s remaining strongholds were no longer on land, but *offshore*—on retrofitted oil platforms, massive desalination barges, and floating industrial archipelagos anchored to the ocean floor.

Yet, for those who lived in the wind-scoured steel towers of the offshore settlements, one ghost loomed larger than all others: Venice.

Before the apocalypse, Venice was a city that flirted with the water, surviving on wooden piles driven into mud, dancing a centuries-long waltz with the tides. When the seas rose, it did not crumble into rubble like the concrete jungles of New York or Tokyo. It simply sank into the emerald depths, intact, becoming a submerged cathedral of memory.

From Rig Zero, a small crew of scavengers set out in a hybrid skiff, cutting through the chop toward the dead zone. Their target was the flooded ruins. 

As the skiff neared the coordinates, the ocean’s depth abruptly plummeted. Below the clear water, the outlines of the ancient city emerged like a drowned Atlantis. It was a haunting sight. The bell tower of St. Mark’s—the *Campanile*—breached the surface like a lonely spire of stone, its tip encrusted with salt and barnacles, serving as the only marker of a vanished world.

The skiff anchored to the upper arches of the Doge’s Palace. A diver named Lorenzo pulled on his rebreather and rolled over the side into the cool, silent sea. 

To dive into Venice after the apocalypse was to enter a frozen dream. Sunlight filtered through twenty meters of green water, casting shimmering beams across the Piazza San Marco. Schools of silvery fish darted through the open arcades where tourists once drank espresso. Sea anemones bloomed like velvet flowers along the marble pillars, and seaweed swayed in the gentle current like the long hair of drowned saints.

Lorenzo swam through the shattered stained-glass windows of the Basilica. Above him, the famous gold-leaf mosaics still caught the dim underwater light, glinting with forgotten majesty. He wasn't there for gold, though; gold was worthless on the offshore rigs. He was searching for brass fittings, intact glass, and historical artifacts that the enclave elders would trade for fresh water and solar batteries.

He paused outside the Rialto Bridge, now a dark arch spanning a canal of deep, silent abyss. In this drowned museum, the apocalypse felt strangely serene. There were no blackened ruins or ash-choked skies—only the peaceful triumph of nature over human ambition. Venice had always belonged to the sea; the sea had simply come to collect its debt.

After securing a haul of bronze lanterns, Lorenzo surfaced near the skiff. He climbed aboard, dripping salt, and looked back toward the open ocean, where the dark silhouette of the offshore rig stood on the horizon against a bruised sunset.

Up there, on the steel platforms, life was a daily battle for survival against rust, hunger, and storms. But down here, in the drowned heart of Venice, the world was at peace. 

As the skiff’s engine hummed to life, heading back to the industrial sanctuary of the offshore world, Lorenzo looked down one last time. Beneath the waves, the Queen of the Adriatic lay waiting, resting in the deep blue quiet of the end of the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark prose poem about being a tourist in flooded Venice, blending imagery of Saint Mark's Basilica, Byzantine plunder, and the Last Judgment mosaics of Torcello.
counterfactuals.output:
We stalk the wooden gangways suspended over a drowning republic, our legs swaddled in garish, yellow plastic—tourists wading through the dark, warm grease of the Adriatic. The air sirens howl their three-toned psalm of *acqua alta*, a mournful liturgy for a city strangling on its own reflection. Below us, the black water laps at the marble skirts of the palazzi, carrying fuel slicks, crushed espresso cups, and the dissolved salt of ten thousand forgotten prayers. We have paid for this front-row seat to the deluge, eager to watch the sea repossess its stolen mud.

In the gloom of Saint Mark’s, the *Chiesa d’Oro* stands knee-deep in its own mirror. The golden vaults sweat brine. We gawk at the sacred spoils of 1204: the four bronze horses, looted from the Hippodrome of Constantinople, suspended in mid-trot above a flooded piazza as if trying to leap out of history; the dark red Tetrarchs clutching one another in porphyry terror against the basilica’s corner, petrified by the rising tide. This sanctuary is a magnificent reliquary of pillage, built on bones smuggled in barrels of lard and marble dragged from the burning ruins of Byzantium. Now, the ocean claims its tithe. The intricate mosaic floor—a carpet of porphyry and serpentine—heaves and ripples like the back of a leviathan waking beneath our boots.

The truth of this place was never in the gold, but buried in the salt-marshes of Torcello, where the great west wall of the cathedral holds the Last Judgment in cold, glittering tesserae. There, the blue-skinned demons of the abyss stoke fires filled with the skulls of kings, and the sea is forced to vomit up its dead—whales spilling pale, half-digested sailors back into the hands of archangels. 

For centuries, Venice painted her own damnation on the wall, and now the mosaic has broken free of its plaster. The sea is no longer yielding the dead; it has come to harvest the living. The water rises through the drain-holes, black and cold, smelling of ancient silt and rot. We raise our glowing smartphones to capture the weeping angels, our shadows stretching monstrously across the gilded domes. We are the final, smiling pilgrims of the apocalypse, floating in plastic boots over sunken empires, waiting for the scales to balance, while the tide ascends the marble stairs to kiss the feet of the Judge.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an atmospheric, literary poem set in late 1990s Venice during high tide, exploring themes of religion, conquest, tourists, and the Doge's ceremony of marrying the sea.
counterfactuals.output:
The sirens blow their three-toned warning call
across November, nineteen-ninety-nine.
The century is aging in its damp, silk sleeves;
the lagoon rises, step by icy step, to dine.
Upon the *passerelle*, the narrow wooden tracks,
the new conquerors march in yellow plastic boots—
a crowd of ghost-light flashes, disposable Kodaks
clicking at the water as it drowns the marble roots.

They have invaded without cannons, without pikes,
armed with pastel raincoats and paper Italian Lira,
wading through the flooded Piazza where the shadow strikes
the bell tower, mirrored in a black, trembling mirror.
They come to consume the corpse before it sinks,
to buy blown-glass tear-drops on the Rialto bridge,
while underneath, the ancient sewage stinks
and salt rots the stucco on each palace ledge.

Here lies the merchant-state that sacked the East,
that dragged four bronze horses from Byzantium’s gate.
The lion of Saint Mark, with stone wings greased
by rain, watches the water reclaim the state.
For every altar plundered, every holy relic torn
from Levant shores to fill a gilded shrine,
the Adriatic sends her tides, solemn and reborn,
to wash the incense from the consecrated pine.

Inside San Marco, the mosaic angels shine
above three inches of dark, encroaching sea.
The apostles drown slowly from the ankles down;
the crypt becomes a hall of cold, wet liturgy.
Holy water meets the brackish, rising flood—
a quiet blasphemy that no priest can stem.
The faith that built this vault out of stone and blood
is now a floating wreath upon the water's hem.

*“Desponsamus te, mare,”* the Doge once cried,
leaning from the red barge, casting down his gold,
marrying the Adriatic as a subjugated bride,
promising dominion over depths untamed and cold.
He threw a ring into the waves to seal the vow,
a gesture of empire, arrogant and grand.
But a marriage is a contract, and the bride is hungry now;
she has come to take the bridegroom by the hand.

She wants no ring of gold; she wants the stone,
the altars, the palazzi, the gondola’s dark prow.
She wants the silver coins, the conqueror's throne,
and the century that falters on its threshold now.
Night falls on the square. The tide begins to crest.
The tourists retreat to hotels warm and bright,
leaving Venice to her husband’s endless, wet chest,
drowning in the dark, bathed in holy, saltwater light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of poetic prose set inside San Marco in Venice. Focus on the flooded marble, the rubies on Christ's mosaic, and the cynicism of modern tourism in a holy place built on ancient plunder.
counterfactuals.output:
The sea does not knock at the doors of San Marco; it slips across the threshold like a thief returning to a house built on theft. 

Here, the pavement does not hold still. The marble floor, worn into petrified waves by centuries of frantic knees, is drowned in three inches of cold, brackish tide. The lagoon has come inside to claim its reflection. In the dark, rising water, the basilica is inverted—a second, subterranean cathedral made of liquid gold and trembling shadows, where the sunken columns seem to reach down into the abyss.

Look up, past the dark tide, into the cavernous vaults where Byzantium came to die and be reborn in gold. Above the wet gloom hangs the Christ Pantocrator, a giant of shimmering *tesserae* suspended in an eternal, unblinking glare. In his halo, set deep within the glittering field of glass and leaf, glow the rubies. They are not merely stones; they are suspended drops of arterial light, dark as pomegranate seeds, catching the dim candle-glow and bleeding into the shadows. They glint with a cold, terrifying majesty—the jewels of a king whose kingdom was bought with the blood of a sacked Constantinople, whose sacred face was pieced together from the shattered majesty of the East.

For this holy place is an ornate chest of stolen treasure. Every slab of green porphyry, every veined marble wall, every fragment of jasper was pried from the bones of older, truer sanctuaries by crusaders who traded their faith for imperial loot. San Marco is a monument to divine plunder, a gilded cage built to house stolen bones and borrowed glory. 

Yet today, the sacrilege is of a cheaper kind.

On the temporary wooden boardwalks elevated above the flooded floor, the modern pilgrims shuffle in a dense, damp herd. They wear neon plastic ponchos that rustle like dry leaves, their faces illuminated not by the rubies of the mosaic, but by the pale, cold glare of three hundred raised smartphones. There is no awe here, only a frantic, transactional urgency to document that they were present at a place they are not actually seeing. 

A guide barks dry facts into a crackling headset; a tourist complains loudly in French about the salt-water ruining her leather boots. A shutter clicks, capturing the burning rubies on the mosaic Christ, while the hands holding the camera never once look up to meet His eyes. They pay their euro-coins for entrance, rush past the drowned history, and retreat into the Piazza to buy plastic gondolas made in distant factories.

Below them, unseen and unheeded, the lagoon continues to rise. It licks at the bases of the stolen columns, eroding the marble, drinking the reflection of the crimson stones. The rubies burn on in the gilded darkness above, untouched by the water, indifferent to the crowds—waiting patiently for the tide to finally take the church, the city, and the slow, cynical world that forgot how to kneel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem about Venice, faith, and the apocalypse.
counterfactuals.output:
The Adriatic breaks its ancient vow,
And swallows up the palace and the spire.
Piazza San Marco is an ocean now,
Reflecting heavens choked in smoke and fire.

The Winged Lion bows his heavy bronze head,
As seventh-trumpet blasts shake the lagoon.
The dark waters rise for the living and dead,
Beneath the pale blood of a dying red moon.

Inside the Basilica, black tides creep
To kiss the gold feet of the saints on the wall.
The doges and martyrs are stirred from their sleep,
To witness the grandest, the finalest fall.

Yet patriarchs kneel on the submerged stone,
With water that reaches the collar and chin,
Lifting their chalices, high and alone,
To offer the world one last cleansing from sin.

The gondolas drift like the coffins of kings,
The Rialto snaps in the apocalyptic swell,
While high in the tempest, an archangel sings
A requiem sweeter than any church bell.

Is it wrath, is it grace, this judgment of brine?
This city of glass turned to bubbles and mist?
Though heaven collapses on all that’s divine,
Faith holds its breath in the deep, un-dismissed.

For far beneath waves where the pale icons shine,
In the drowned, silent dark, the stone apostles still pray,
Waiting for Venice—and sea—to divine
The glorious dawn of the Eighth, Endless Day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw, vivid poem inspired by the ekphrastic tradition, written from the perspective of someone standing ankle-deep in the Adriatic inside a Venetian church, reflecting on how Christ is portrayed in Byzantine mosaics versus how tourists view him.
counterfactuals.output:
Brackish and thick, the Adriatic licks my achilles,
sloshing through the heavy bronze doors,
carrying the rot of eel-grass, diesel, and dead crabs
across centuries of sunken marble.
My shoes are ruined. Salt eats through the leather,
stinging where the cold tide climbs my shins,
while overhead, suspended in a vault of fired clay and leaf,
the vault burns with four million pieces of glass.

Look at Him up there in the apse.
He is not the sweet milk-boy of the later oil painters.
He is the *Pantokrator*—an iron-jawed emperor smashed into gold,
stitched together with mortar and hammer-stroke.
His eyes are asymmetric, huge and black:
one wide with terrifying mercy,
the other narrowed to measure the marrow of your spine.
His fingers do not reach out to comfort;
they are hooked in judgment, heavy as anvil-iron,
holding a book bound in blood-red tesserae.
He is flat, severe, ancient—
a God forged when men knew light was a fire that consumed you,
a tyrant of grace who demands you hit the wet stone on your knees.

Behind me, the water splashes.
A flock of yellow rain-ponchos sloshes through the aisle.
Plastic-wrapped boots squeak against the drowned mosaic floor.
A hundred tiny screens rise up like blue fireflies.

*Look at the color palette,* someone whispers, adjusting a lens.
*The flat perspective is so typical of the eleventh century.*
*Can you get a shot without the glare?*

They consume Him in megabytes.
They flatten the Judge into a souvenir,
a postcard to slide between a plate of cuttlefish
and a photo of the Rialto at dusk.
They see an artifact surviving bad plumbing.
They see "style." They see "heritage."
They want Him cute. They want Him contextualized.
They want a God who fits neatly into a ten-minute walkthrough
before the tide gets too high for lunch.

They do not feel the sea creeping up their ribs.
They do not see that the water in this nave is not an accident—
it is His hand unmaking the city.
The tesserae flicker in the dark vault,
refused by their digital sensors, spilling gold into the brackish scum.

I stand here, my feet numbing in the dark brine,
and stare back into those uneven, terrifying eyes.
He does not look at their cameras.
He looks past us all, out toward the Lagoon,
watching the ocean swallow His altar,
unblinking, unpitying,
waiting for the water to reach His knees.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
